specStatements.text: The main energy resources available for use on Earth include: fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves.
A renewable energy resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.
The uses of energy resources include: transport, electricity generation and heating.
• describe the main energy sources available
• distinguish between energy resources that are renewable and energy resources that are non-renewable
• compare ways that different energy resources are used, the uses to include transport, electricity generation and heating
• understand why some energy resources are more reliable than others
• describe the environmental impact arising from the use of different energy resources
• explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources.
Descriptions of how energy resources are used to generate electricity are not required.
• consider the environmental issues that may arise from the use of different energy resources

• show that science has the ability to identify environmental issues arising from the use of energy resources but not always the power to deal with the issues because of political, social, ethical or economic considerations.

scopeNotes.statement: Descriptions of how energy resources are used to generate electricity are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item in this section describes the machinery by which a resource is turned into electricity. There is no boiler, no steam cycle, no turbine, no generator, no photovoltaic cell and no tidal barrage anywhere in the concepts, misconceptions or questions. Resources are named, sorted into renewable and non-renewable, matched to the three listed uses, compared for reliability and judged for environmental impact - all of which the specification does require. Where a resource has to be identified, it is identified by where its energy comes from (hot rock, moving air, stored water, sunlight, the rise and fall of the sea), never by the internal working of a power station. Question q09 deliberately stops at 'this is heating, not electricity generation' and does not go on to say how a panel would have made electricity.

concepts.definition: A supply of energy that people can draw on. The main energy resources available for use on Earth include fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves. Electricity is not an energy resource: it has to be generated using one of these resources.

The three fossil fuels named by the specification. They formed from the remains of living things over many millions of years and are burned to release energy. They are non-renewable: they are not replenished on any timescale that matters against the rate at which they are used.
Uranium (or plutonium) used as a fuel in nuclear power stations. It is mined from rock but it is not a fossil fuel, and it is non-renewable because the fuel is not replenished as it is used.
Fuel made from plant or animal material, for example wood, crops grown for fuel, or waste. It is renewable because the crops used can be grown again as the fuel is used.

Moving air, used as an energy resource mainly for electricity generation. It is renewable, and it is unreliable in the sense that its output rises and falls with the weather and cannot be turned up on demand.

An energy resource that uses water stored behind a dam, usually in a river valley. It is renewable, because rain refills the reservoir, and it is comparatively reliable because the stored water can be released when it is wanted.
An energy resource that uses the energy of hot rock beneath the Earth's surface. It is renewable and available at all hours, but it is only practical where hot rock lies close enough to the surface.

The twice-daily rise and fall of the sea, caused by the Moon and the Sun rather than by the weather. Tidal energy is renewable and reliable, because the times of high and low water are known in advance.

The Sun is an energy resource in its own right. Its energy can be used for heating (for example warming water directly) as well as for electricity generation. It is renewable, and its output varies with the time of day, the season and the cloud.
Waves on the surface of the sea, raised by the wind. Wave energy is renewable and is a separate resource from both hydro-electricity and the tides.

A renewable energy resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used. The test is replacement keeping pace with use - not the size of the supply, not the price, and not whether the resource is clean.
A resource that is not replenished as it is used, so the supply falls as it is drawn on. Coal, oil, gas and nuclear fuel are non-renewable.
Moving people and goods. Worldwide, transport runs overwhelmingly on oil, as petrol and diesel; bio-fuel and electricity supply smaller shares.
Producing electricity for the mains supply. Almost every resource on the specification's list can be used this way, which is why electricity itself is not a resource.
Warming homes, water and industrial processes. Gas, oil, bio-fuel, geothermal and the Sun are all used for heating directly, without any electricity being generated first.

How dependably a resource can supply energy when it is wanted. Fossil fuels, nuclear fuel and geothermal can be run whenever they are needed; the tides are predictable in advance; wind, the Sun and water waves depend on the weather. Reliability is about availability on demand, not about how much energy the resource gives out.

The damage done by obtaining and using a resource: carbon dioxide from burning fuels, sulfur dioxide leading to acid rain, radioactive waste from nuclear fuel, and land, habitat and landscape effects from dams, wind farms and fuel crops. Every resource has some impact.

concepts.term: Trends in the use of energy resources
concepts.definition: Patterns over time, such as the rising share of wind and solar, the decline of coal, and the continued dominance of oil in transport. Trends are driven by cost, by concern about environmental impact and by government decisions.

concepts.term: Political, social, ethical and economic considerations
concepts.definition: The non-scientific factors that decide whether an environmental issue is acted on. Science can identify an issue but does not always have the power to deal with it, because cost, jobs, public opinion, fairness between countries and government policy all bear on what is actually done.

misconceptions.question: Does calling a resource renewable mean it can never run out?
misconceptions.correct: A renewable resource is one that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used.
misconceptions.misconception: Renewable means the supply is unlimited, so it can be used at any rate for ever.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday word suggests endlessness, and students meet it alongside slogans such as 'the wind will always blow'.
misconceptions.correction: The specification's test is replacement, not size. Bio-fuel is renewable only because the crops are grown again; stop replanting and it runs out.

misconceptions.question: Is a resource renewable because it releases no carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: Renewable and clean are different ideas: nuclear fuel releases no carbon dioxide but is non-renewable, and bio-fuel releases carbon dioxide but is renewable.
misconceptions.misconception: Renewable resources are the clean ones, so anything that gives off no carbon dioxide must be renewable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Renewables are advertised as the green choice, so students merge 'clean' and 'renewable' into one category.
misconceptions.correction: Ask only one question: is it being replenished as it is used? Answer that first, then treat environmental impact as a separate judgement.

misconceptions.question: Does renewable mean the energy is free?
misconceptions.correct: Renewable describes replenishment, not price. Wind farms and dams cost a great deal to build.
misconceptions.misconception: A renewable resource costs nothing, because nobody has to pay for the wind or the sunlight.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear that the fuel is free and generalise it to the whole resource.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the fuel cost from the classification. The definition says nothing about money.

misconceptions.question: Is electricity one of the main energy resources?
misconceptions.correct: Electricity is not an energy resource: it has to be generated using a resource such as coal, wind or the tides.
misconceptions.misconception: Electricity is an energy resource in its own right, alongside coal and wind.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electricity arrives at a socket like a supply, and students meet 'electrical energy' constantly, so it feels like a source.
misconceptions.correction: Trace it back one step: every unit of electricity came from a resource on the specification's list.

misconceptions.question: Is a wind turbine an energy resource?
misconceptions.correct: The resource is the wind; the turbine is the equipment used to make use of it.
misconceptions.misconception: Wind turbines, solar panels and dams are themselves energy resources.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The machinery is the visible thing, so students name the hardware rather than the supply it draws on.
misconceptions.correction: Name the supply, not the device: wind, the Sun, stored water.

misconceptions.question: Is geothermal energy really energy from the Sun?
misconceptions.correct: Geothermal energy comes from hot rock beneath the surface, not from sunlight warming the ground.
misconceptions.misconception: The ground is warm because the Sun has been shining on it, so geothermal is a form of solar energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the Sun warms the ground and reason that all underground warmth must have the same origin.
misconceptions.correction: Geothermal wells reach rock that is hot far below the depth sunlight has any effect on.

misconceptions.question: Does geothermal energy come from burning something underground?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing is burned. The rock underground is already hot, and that is the resource.
misconceptions.misconception: Geothermal energy comes from fuel burning deep inside the Earth.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'energy from the ground' with coal, oil and gas, which do come from underground.
misconceptions.correction: Geothermal is renewable precisely because there is no fuel being consumed.

misconceptions.question: Is nuclear fuel a fossil fuel?
misconceptions.correct: The fossil fuels are only coal, oil and gas. Nuclear fuel is a separate non-renewable resource.
misconceptions.misconception: Uranium is dug out of the ground like coal, so nuclear fuel is one of the fossil fuels.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Mined from rock' is taken as the definition of a fossil fuel instead of 'formed from the remains of living things'.
misconceptions.correction: Both are non-renewable, but for the classification question the list of fossil fuels is fixed at three.

misconceptions.question: Do nuclear power stations release carbon dioxide as they run?
misconceptions.correct: They do not burn a fuel, so no carbon dioxide is released; their characteristic impact is radioactive waste.
misconceptions.misconception: Nuclear stations pour clouds out of huge towers, so they must be releasing carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The cooling-tower plume looks like smoke; it is condensed water vapour.
misconceptions.correction: Match each impact to its cause: carbon dioxide comes from burning, radioactive waste comes from nuclear fuel.

misconceptions.question: Is bio-fuel non-renewable because burning it gives off carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: Bio-fuel is renewable, because the crops it is made from can be grown again as the fuel is used.
misconceptions.misconception: Bio-fuel burns and gives off carbon dioxide just as coal does, so it must be non-renewable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students classify by what happens at the moment of use rather than by whether the supply is replaced.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the definition to the supply, not to the exhaust. New crops replace the fuel; new coal does not.

misconceptions.question: New coal is still forming, so is coal renewable?
misconceptions.correct: Coal is non-renewable: it forms far more slowly than it is being used.
misconceptions.misconception: Coal is being replenished underground all the time, so it counts as renewable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'replenished' is read as 'any replacement at all', with no attention to rate.
misconceptions.correction: Replenishment has to keep pace with use. Coal takes millions of years to form and is burned in a moment.

misconceptions.question: Are lighting and cooking two of the three uses named by the specification?
misconceptions.correct: The three uses given are transport, electricity generation and heating.
misconceptions.misconception: The listed uses are transport, lighting and cooking, because that is what energy is used for at home.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students substitute familiar household jobs for the specification's broader categories.
misconceptions.correction: Lighting and cooking sit inside the listed categories - they are things done with electricity or with heating.

misconceptions.question: Does an electric car use no energy resource?
misconceptions.correct: It uses whatever resource generated its electricity, which worldwide is still mostly fossil fuels.
misconceptions.misconception: An electric car burns no fuel, so it uses no energy resource and has no environmental impact.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nothing is burned at the car, so the impact of generating the electricity is invisible to the user.
misconceptions.correction: Follow the chain back to the power station: the resource used is the one that made the electricity.

misconceptions.question: Is every solar panel generating electricity?
misconceptions.correct: The Sun is used both for heating directly, such as warming water on a roof, and for electricity generation.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything solar on a roof makes electricity, so the Sun's only use is electricity generation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Solar panel' is used loosely for two different things, and electricity is the use students hear about.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what comes out: hot water means the use is heating; a supply to the mains means electricity generation.

misconceptions.question: Can any resource on the list be used for any of the three uses?
misconceptions.correct: Resources differ: oil dominates transport, while wind and the tides are used almost entirely for electricity generation.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy is energy, so any resource could be used for transport, heating or electricity generation equally.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The idea that energy can be transferred in many ways is over-generalised into 'every resource suits every job'.
misconceptions.correction: Compare actual uses. You cannot run a lorry off a tidal stream, and nobody heats a house with uranium.

misconceptions.question: Is wind reliable because the wind never completely stops?
misconceptions.correct: Wind is unreliable: its output falls when the wind drops, whatever the demand happens to be.
misconceptions.misconception: The wind is always blowing somewhere, so wind can be counted on at any time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience of breezy days, plus the fact that turbines are often turning, hides the calm periods.
misconceptions.correction: Reliability means available when it is wanted. A calm, cold evening is exactly when demand is high and wind output is low.

misconceptions.question: Does reliable mean the resource gives out a lot of energy?
misconceptions.correct: Reliability is about availability on demand, not about output. A small geothermal plant is reliable; a huge wind farm is not.
misconceptions.misconception: The reliable resources are the powerful ones that supply the most energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Reliable' is treated as a general word of praise and merged with 'big' or 'good'.
misconceptions.correction: Judge reliability by one question only: can it supply energy whenever it is wanted?

misconceptions.question: Are wind and solar unreliable because the equipment breaks down?
misconceptions.correct: They are unreliable because the wind and the sunshine vary, not because the machinery is faulty.
misconceptions.misconception: Turbines and panels are badly made and keep failing, which is why they are called unreliable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Unreliable' in everyday speech means 'keeps going wrong', so the fault is placed on the hardware.
misconceptions.correction: The turbine works perfectly on a calm day; there is simply no wind for it to use.

misconceptions.question: Are the tides caused by the weather?
misconceptions.correct: The tides are caused by the Moon and the Sun, and rise and fall on a known cycle.
misconceptions.misconception: The tides are part of the sea, and the sea is driven by the wind, so tidal energy is as unpredictable as wind.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Waves and tides are both movements of the sea and get merged into one idea.
misconceptions.correction: Tide tables are printed years ahead. That predictability is exactly why tidal energy counts as reliable.

misconceptions.question: Does carbon dioxide cause acid rain?
misconceptions.correct: Acid rain comes mainly from sulfur dioxide released when fuels containing sulfur are burned.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is the pollutant from burning fuels, so it must cause acid rain as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon dioxide is the only combustion product many students can name, so it is blamed for every effect.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two apart: carbon dioxide contributes to global warming; sulfur dioxide causes acid rain.

misconceptions.question: Do renewable resources have no environmental impact?
misconceptions.correct: Every resource has some impact: dams flood land, wind farms change landscapes and habitats, fuel crops take land that could grow food.
misconceptions.misconception: Renewables are the green option, so using them does no environmental damage at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Renewables are presented as the solution to pollution, and 'less impact' is heard as 'no impact'.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what had to be built or grown, and what land was used, before deciding a resource is harmless.

misconceptions.question: Have wind and solar already replaced fossil fuels?
misconceptions.correct: Fossil fuels still supply most of the world's energy, especially for transport and heating.
misconceptions.misconception: Renewables have taken over, so fossil fuels are basically finished as an energy resource.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rapid growth in renewable electricity is reported constantly, and electricity is mistaken for all energy use.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the trend from the total: a fast-growing share can still be a small share.

misconceptions.question: Will science solve an environmental issue once it has identified it?
misconceptions.correct: Science can identify an issue but does not always have the power to deal with it, because of political, social, ethical or economic considerations.
misconceptions.misconception: Once scientists have shown what the problem is, the problem will be fixed; it is only a matter of time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: School science is presented as a sequence of problems solved, so identifying and solving look like the same step.
misconceptions.correction: Cost, jobs, public opinion and international agreement all decide what is actually done with what science has shown.

misconceptions.question: Are we changing away from fossil fuels only because they are running out?
misconceptions.correct: The change is driven mainly by concern about environmental impact and by the falling cost of wind and solar.
misconceptions.misconception: We are moving to renewables because the coal, oil and gas have nearly all been used up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Non-renewable' is heard as 'about to run out', so scarcity is assumed to be the driver.
misconceptions.correction: Known reserves are still large. It is impact and cost, not exhaustion, that explain the recent trend.

mcqs.stem: A student is asked to list the main energy resources available for use on Earth. Which list is correct?

options.text: Nuclear fuel, the tides, geothermal energy and water waves
options.rationale: All four appear in the specification's list of the main energy resources available for use on Earth.

options.text: Bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity and mains electricity
options.rationale: Three are resources, but electricity is not one: it has to be generated using a resource, so it cannot appear on the list.

options.text: Coal, oil, gas and the steam produced in a boiler
options.rationale: Steam is not a resource either. It is something produced when a fuel is used, so the student has confused a stage of use with a supply.

options.text: The Sun, wind turbines, the tides and bio-fuel crops
options.rationale: Names the machinery instead of the supply. The resource is the wind; the turbine is the equipment that makes use of it.

mcqs.stem: Where does the energy supplied by a geothermal resource come from?

options.text: From sunlight that has warmed the ground during the day
options.rationale: The Sun does warm the surface, but geothermal wells reach far below any depth sunlight affects.

options.text: From the hot rock lying deep below the Earth's surface
options.rationale: Geothermal energy is the energy of hot rock underground, which is why it is available at all hours and in any weather.

options.text: From fossil fuels that are burning deep underground
options.rationale: Nothing is burned. Treating geothermal as a hidden fuel would also make it non-renewable, which it is not.

options.text: From friction as the Earth spins on its axis each day
options.rationale: A plausible-sounding mechanical origin, but it is not the source; the rock is already hot.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is the specification's definition of a renewable energy resource?

options.text: One with a supply so large that it could never all be used up
options.rationale: Makes the test the size of the store. Bio-fuel's supply is not huge; it is renewable because crops are regrown.

options.text: One that gives off no carbon dioxide while it is being used
options.rationale: Confuses clean with renewable. Nuclear fuel gives off no carbon dioxide and is non-renewable.

options.text: One that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used
options.rationale: This is the definition word for word: replacement keeping pace with use.

options.text: One that costs nothing to use once it has been built
options.rationale: Price is not part of the definition, and a wind farm is expensive to build.

mcqs.stem: Nuclear fuel is classified as non-renewable. Which reason for that classification is correct?

options.text: Uranium is mined from rock, so it is a fossil fuel
options.rationale: Right label, wrong route. The fossil fuels are only coal, oil and gas; being mined does not make a fuel fossil.

options.text: Nuclear power stations release carbon dioxide as they run
options.rationale: They burn nothing, so no carbon dioxide is released - and carbon dioxide is not the renewable test anyway.

options.text: Its waste stays radioactive for a very long time indeed
options.rationale: A true statement about environmental impact, but impact is a separate judgement from the renewable classification.

options.text: The uranium used is not replenished as it is used
options.rationale: Applies the definition directly: the fuel in the ground is not being replaced as it is consumed.

mcqs.stem: Why is bio-fuel classified as a renewable energy resource?

options.text: The crops it is made from can be grown again as the fuel is used
options.rationale: The definition is met: the supply is replenished, by replanting, at the rate it is drawn on.

options.text: It gives off much less carbon dioxide than burning coal does
options.rationale: An environmental claim, not the classification test. Bio-fuel does release carbon dioxide when burned.

options.text: There is so much plant material that it could never run out
options.rationale: Treats renewable as meaning an unlimited store. Without replanting, bio-fuel would run out.

options.text: It is made from living things rather than from rock
options.rationale: Coal also formed from living things and is non-renewable, so origin cannot be the test.

mcqs.stem: New coal is still slowly forming underground today. Why is coal still classed as non-renewable?

options.text: It is not: coal is renewable because new coal is still forming
options.rationale: Reads 'replenished' as any replacement at all, ignoring rate, which is the whole point of the definition.

options.text: New coal is forming far more slowly than it is being used
options.rationale: Replenishment has to keep pace with use. Coal takes millions of years to form and is burned in minutes.

options.text: Coal gives off carbon dioxide, and renewables are clean
options.rationale: Uses environmental impact as the classification test. Bio-fuel also releases carbon dioxide and is renewable.

options.text: Coal supplies will have run out within about ten years
options.rationale: Non-renewable does not mean nearly exhausted; large reserves remain, but they are not being replaced.

mcqs.stem: The specification gives three uses of energy resources. Which set of three is correct?

options.text: Transport, electricity generation and lighting
options.rationale: Lighting is something done with electricity once it has been generated, not a separate listed use.

options.text: Electricity generation, heating and cooking food
options.rationale: Cooking sits inside heating; the specification's categories are broader than household jobs.

options.text: Transport, electricity generation and heating
options.rationale: These are the three uses named in the specification.

options.text: Heating, lighting and cooking in the home
options.rationale: These are jobs done in a house using electricity or heating; they are not the specification's three categories.

mcqs.stem: Which energy resource supplies most of the energy used for transport worldwide?

options.text: Electricity from wind farms
options.rationale: Electric vehicles are growing quickly but still carry a small fraction of the world's transport.

options.text: Bio-fuel grown from sugar cane
options.rationale: Bio-fuel is used in transport, but it is a minor contribution beside oil.

options.text: Coal burned in steam engines
options.rationale: Coal moved trains a century ago; it is not the main transport resource now.

options.text: Oil, as petrol and diesel
options.rationale: Transport runs overwhelmingly on oil products; other resources supply only small shares.

mcqs.stem: Panels on the roof of a house use the Sun to warm the water in a hot water tank. Which use of an energy resource is this?

options.text: Heating, because the Sun's energy is warming the water directly
options.rationale: The resource is the Sun and the job being done is heating; no electricity is involved at any point.

options.text: Electricity generation, because solar panels make electricity
options.rationale: Assumes every roof panel is a photovoltaic one. These panels deliver hot water, not a supply to the mains.

options.text: Transport, because the hot water is moved along pipes
options.rationale: Transport means moving people and goods, not moving water within a building.

options.text: Electricity generation, then heating from the mains
options.rationale: Adds a generation stage that does not exist here; the Sun warms the water directly.

mcqs.stem: Which group of resources is used for all three of transport, electricity generation and heating?

options.text: Wind, which could drive vehicles, power stations and radiators
options.rationale: Wind is used almost entirely for electricity generation; it does not drive vehicles or heat homes.

options.text: Fossil fuels, which are burned for all three of these jobs
options.rationale: Oil fuels transport, gas and coal generate electricity, and gas and oil heat buildings.

options.text: The tides, which run at all hours and serve every use
options.rationale: Predictable, but tidal energy is used for electricity generation only.

options.text: Nuclear fuel, used in stations, cars and in boilers
options.rationale: Nuclear fuel is used in power stations; no car or domestic boiler runs on it.

mcqs.stem: Why is a wind farm a less reliable energy resource than a gas-fired power station?

options.text: It is not less reliable, because the wind never stops blowing
options.rationale: Calm periods are real, and they can coincide with the coldest, highest-demand evenings.

options.text: Each turbine gives out less energy than a gas power station
options.rationale: Confuses reliability with size of output; a small geothermal plant is reliable despite being small.

options.text: Its output falls when the wind drops, whatever the demand
options.rationale: Reliability is about being available when energy is wanted, and wind output is set by the weather.

options.text: Wind turbines break down far more often than gas plants
options.rationale: Blames the hardware. The turbine works perfectly on a calm day; there is simply no wind.

mcqs.stem: Tidal energy is described as a reliable energy resource. Which statement explains why?

options.text: The tides are driven by winds that blow daily
options.rationale: Waves are raised by the wind; the tides are not, which is exactly why they are predictable.

options.text: Tidal stations give out more energy than any other
options.rationale: Reliability is about availability on demand, not about how much energy is supplied.

options.text: The sea is always deep, so the water never stops
options.rationale: The sea being present is not the point; a resource is reliable when its supply can be counted on.

options.text: The tides rise and fall on a known cycle
options.rationale: The times of high and low water are set by the Moon and the Sun and can be predicted years ahead.

mcqs.stem: Which environmental impact arises directly from burning fossil fuels in a power station?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide are released into the air
options.rationale: Burning releases carbon dioxide, which contributes to global warming, and sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain.

options.text: Radioactive waste is produced and has to be stored safely
options.rationale: That is the characteristic impact of nuclear fuel, not of burning coal, oil or gas.

options.text: The steam from the cooling towers poisons nearby land
options.rationale: The plume from a cooling tower is condensed water vapour, not a pollutant.

options.text: Acid rain is formed by the carbon dioxide given off
options.rationale: Names the wrong gas. Acid rain comes mainly from sulfur dioxide.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the environmental impact of renewable energy resources is correct?

options.text: They cause no environmental damage of any kind at all
options.rationale: Treats renewable as a guarantee of harmlessness; every resource has to be built, grown or installed somewhere.

options.text: They have impacts too, such as land flooded behind a hydro dam
options.rationale: Renewable does not mean harmless: dams flood valleys, wind farms alter landscapes and habitats, fuel crops use land.

options.text: Bio-fuel is the one renewable that has no effect at all on land use
options.rationale: Bio-fuel crops take land that could otherwise grow food or support habitats.

options.text: Their only impact is the carbon dioxide released in use
options.rationale: Wind, hydro and tidal resources release no carbon dioxide in use, yet they still have impacts.

mcqs.stem: The share of UK electricity generated from renewable resources has risen sharply since 2010. Which explanation of this trend is best?

options.text: The UK's coal, oil and gas have now all been used up
options.rationale: Reserves are still substantial; exhaustion is not what caused the recent shift.

options.text: Renewables can now supply power at all times without any backup
options.rationale: Wind and solar output still varies with the weather, so other resources are still needed.

options.text: Concern about carbon dioxide, and cheaper wind and solar
options.rationale: Environmental concern plus falling cost is what has driven the change, supported by government policy.

options.text: Fossil fuels have been replaced completely across all energy use
options.rationale: Fossil fuels still supply most transport and heating; the change is in electricity, and it is partial.

mcqs.stem: Scientists identified the harm caused by burning fossil fuels many years ago, yet their use has continued. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: The evidence is still too uncertain for anyone to act on it
options.rationale: The issue has been identified; the delay is not caused by the science being unsettled.

options.text: Scientists have not yet explained the harm to any government
options.rationale: Governments have been told repeatedly; identifying and communicating an issue is not the obstacle.

options.text: No other energy resource could possibly replace the fossil fuels
options.rationale: Alternatives exist and are growing; the difficulty lies in the cost and pace of changing over.

options.text: Political, social, ethical and economic factors count too
options.rationale: Science can identify an environmental issue but does not always have the power to deal with it; cost, jobs, public opinion and government policy all bear on what is done.
